title: 1031 Exchange Basics
summary: Fundamental training on 1031 exchanges for real estate agents. Covers what a 1031 exchange is, when it applies, the critical rules and timelines (45-day identification, 180-day close), qualified intermediary requirements, like-kind property definition, boot rules, and common mistakes that disqualify the exchange. Includes Utah-specific disclosure forms and practical guidance for working with investor clients.

broker_guidance.scenario: Client asks about 1031 exchange after already selling
broker_guidance.guidance: If client has already closed and received proceeds without a qualified intermediary, they CANNOT do a 1031 exchange. This is the most common fatal mistake. Must be set up BEFORE closing.
broker_guidance.client_language: If you've already closed and have the check in hand, we cannot 1031 exchange that. You needed to set this up before closing with a qualified intermediary.

broker_guidance.scenario: Setting up a 1031 exchange for a client
broker_guidance.guidance: At the very beginning, client needs: (1) Qualified Intermediary, (2) Title company aware of the exchange, (3) Accountant involved for tax planning. Title has specific requirements they need quickly.
broker_guidance.client_language: Before we go any further, we need to get a qualified intermediary involved and make sure the title company knows this is a 1031 exchange. Your accountant should also be looped in.

broker_guidance.guidance: Section 1031 of IRS code governs capital gains taxes. It's a DEFERRAL process - not elimination. Taxes get kicked down the road. IRS created this to encourage investors to stay in the market rather than getting hit with huge tax bills that prevent reinvestment.
broker_guidance.client_language: A 1031 exchange lets you defer paying capital gains tax by reinvesting the proceeds into another investment property. You're not eliminating the tax - just kicking it down the road.

broker_guidance.scenario: Client asks about capital gains rates
broker_guidance.guidance: Short-term (held less than 1 year): Ordinary income rates, 10-37% federal. Long-term (held more than 1 year): 0-20% depending on income bracket. Flippers pay up to 37% - baked into their math. Accountant does the actual math.
broker_guidance.client_language: Short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income - up to 37%. Long-term is 0-20% depending on your tax bracket. Your accountant will calculate the exact amount.

broker_guidance.scenario: Client asks what qualifies as like-kind
broker_guidance.guidance: Like-kind is broad for real estate: Any investment property for any other investment property. Can exchange rental house for commercial building, land for apartment complex, etc. Does NOT include primary residence. Must be investment/business property.
broker_guidance.client_language: Like-kind is very broad for real estate. You can exchange a rental house for commercial property, land for apartments, etc. But it has to be investment property - your primary residence doesn't qualify.

broker_guidance.guidance: From closing of relinquished property, client has 45 calendar days to identify replacement properties. Must be in writing, signed, and delivered to qualified intermediary. Can identify: (A) Up to 3 properties of any value, OR (B) Any number of properties as long as total value doesn't exceed 200% of sold property value, OR (C) Any number if acquiring 95% of identified value.
broker_guidance.client_language: You have 45 days from closing to identify replacement properties in writing. Most people use the 3-property rule - you can list up to 3 properties regardless of their total value.

broker_guidance.guidance: Must close on replacement property within 180 calendar days of closing the relinquished property. This is a hard deadline - no extensions. Must close, not just be under contract.
broker_guidance.client_language: You have 180 days from the sale of your old property to close on the new one. No extensions, no exceptions. We need to be under contract well before that deadline.

broker_guidance.scenario: Client asks about taking cash out (boot)
broker_guidance.guidance: Any cash or debt relief taken out is called 'boot' and is taxable in the year of the exchange. To fully defer ALL taxes, must: (1) Buy replacement property equal or greater in value, AND (2) Reinvest ALL net equity, AND (3) Replace ALL debt. If client takes $50K cash out, they pay tax on $50K but defer the rest.
broker_guidance.client_language: If you take cash out of the deal, that portion is taxable. To defer ALL taxes, you need to buy a property equal or greater in value and put all your equity into it.

broker_guidance.scenario: Client wants to exchange into multiple properties
broker_guidance.guidance: Yes, can exchange one property for multiple replacement properties. Must follow same 45/180 day rules. Can also do reverse exchange (buy new before selling old) but more complex and expensive.
broker_guidance.client_language: Yes, you can buy multiple replacement properties with the proceeds. Same rules apply - 45 days to identify, 180 days to close on all of them.

broker_guidance.guidance: Utah has a specific form for disclosing when a property being sold is part of a 1031 exchange. Buyer must be informed. Form should be in the state-approved documents.
broker_guidance.client_language: Utah requires us to disclose to the buyer that this property is part of a 1031 exchange. There's a specific state form we'll include with the disclosures.

steps: Determine if client has already closed on relinquished property (if yes, too late)
Engage qualified intermediary BEFORE listing or closing
Notify title company that transaction is part of 1031 exchange
Have client consult with accountant for tax planning
List and sell relinquished property - proceeds go to qualified intermediary
Within 45 days of closing, identify replacement properties in writing to QI
Within 180 days of closing, close on replacement property
Ensure replacement value is equal or greater and all equity is reinvested
Complete Utah disclosure form if applicable
File appropriate tax forms with accountant

objections.objection: I already sold my property and have the money
objections.response: Unfortunately, if you've already closed and received the proceeds without a qualified intermediary, you cannot do a 1031 exchange. The QI must be engaged before closing.

The rules are specific but straightforward. The key is having the right team: qualified intermediary, title company, and accountant. They handle the complexity. Your job is finding the replacement property within the timelines.

objections.objection: I want to take some cash out for other things
objections.response: You can, but any cash you take out (called 'boot') is taxable in the year of the exchange. You'll defer taxes on the rest. Many investors do partial exchanges.

objections.objection: What if I can't find a replacement in 45 days?
objections.response: The 45-day identification is strict with no extensions. We need to start looking immediately. Most investors use the 3-property rule and have backups ready.

objections.objection: Can I buy a primary residence with the exchange?
objections.response: No. 1031 exchanges are for investment or business property only. You cannot exchange into a primary residence. However, you could convert an investment property to primary later after meeting holding requirements.
